clue.text: Bern chef cooking hand peeled veg

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be mixed

indicators.note: peeling strips the outer skin, so the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: hand with its outer letters stripped

explanation.surface: A chef in Bern is preparing vegetables by hand, peeling them for the pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A French bean is a green bean eaten as a vegetable, and veg is the casual word for vegetables.

clue.text: Cod fish's head put on headless fish a bit like cod

indicators.note: without a head, the next word loses its opening letter
the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: opening letter
hake is a food fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A cod's head is attached to the body of a similar fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The first Cod is not the fish: as an adjective it means sham, as in cod philosophy.
explanation.definitionFit: Cod in British usage means fake or mock, as in a cod accent.

clue.text: Mission to force into cove sinking steamship

indicators.note: something sinking goes down into another thing, ending up inside it

parts.note: to embay is to drive a ship into a bay
SS is the prefix for steamship

explanation.surface: A naval operation drives an enemy into a bay and sinks their steamer.
explanation.definitionFit: An embassy is a diplomatic mission, the official delegation sent to a foreign country.

clue.text: A red wine one tossed back — 10F almost!

parts.note: a caber is the pole tossed at Highland games

indicators.note: back here means read backwards

parts.note: the number spelt out

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter goes

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for francs

explanation.surface: A glass of red knocked back, and it cost nearly ten francs.
explanation.walkthrough: 10F looks like a cross-reference to 10-across but is ten francs; caber tossing is a Scottish Highland games event.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabernet Franc is a black grape variety and the red wine made from it, grown in Bordeaux and the Loire.

clue.text: Rolls manufacturer taking on occasionally nerdier travel guide

indicators.note: taking on means admitting something within

parts.note: a baker makes bread rolls

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so only alternate letters are kept

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A car maker hires some nerdier staff to produce a guidebook.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolls suggests Rolls-Royce cars, but it is bread rolls.
explanation.definitionFit: Baedeker guidebooks, first published by Karl Baedeker in Germany, became a byword for a tourist handbook.

clue.text: American exhausted after taking time off here in the Rockies

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, here the abbreviation for time

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
spent means worn out

explanation.surface: A tired American takes a holiday in the Rocky Mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspen is a ski resort town in Colorado, in the Rocky Mountains, so a place found there.

clue.text: Facile drivel endlessly circulating

indicators.note: going round in a circle brings the letters back the other way
without an end, the word drops its final letter

parts.note: bilge is nonsense or rubbish talk

explanation.surface: Easy nonsense keeps doing the rounds without ever stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Glib and facile both describe speech that is fluent but shallow and insincere.

clue.text: Mean about poor Jack's reason to visit doctor

indicators.note: about means surrounding, placed on either side

parts.note: low means base or mean

indicators.note: poor suggests something in bad shape, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A stingy person complains about poor Jack needing to see a GP.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is part of the surface and gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lockjaw, a symptom of tetanus that clamps the jaw shut, is a medical condition sending someone to a GP.

clue.text: One who might pull a bob or two at work?

definitions.text: One who might pull a bob or two at work?

parts.note: surface reading: someone pulling in a few shillings, a bob being an old British coin
setter's reading: a bob is a change-ringing method, worked by pulling ropes in a church tower

explanation.walkthrough: A bob was slang for a shilling, so the surface is about earning money; in change ringing a bob is a call that alters the sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Church tower ringers pull ropes to ring methods such as Plain Bob.

clue.text: King rejected young pig put on skewer

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: Babe is the piglet hero of the film, and a babe is a young one

explanation.surface: A king turns down a piglet that has been roasted on a spit.
explanation.definitionFit: To kebab something is to thread it on a skewer for cooking, a verb use of the familiar dish.

clue.text: Repaired replica? I'm using knowledge gained by experience

indicators.note: something repaired has been taken apart and put back together, so the letters are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who fixed up a copy claims to have learned the craft by hands-on practice.
explanation.definitionFit: Empirical knowledge comes from observation and trial rather than from theory.

clue.text: Sellers playing entertaining detective with Yard in a cruel way

indicators.note: to entertain is to host someone, taking them in
playing about with something rearranges it freely

parts.note: taken as written
Inspector Morse, the Oxford TV detective
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: Peter Sellers, cast in a role opposite a Scotland Yard detective, plays it heartlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Sellers played Inspector Clouseau, but Sellers here is just letters; Yard hints at Scotland Yard.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorselessly means without pity or compassion, hence cruelly.

clue.text: Soldier's given a new order to James Garner

indicators.note: putting things in a new order rearranges them, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written, all thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A soldier receives fresh orders addressed to the actor James Garner.
explanation.walkthrough: James Garner was an American actor, here only for his letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant major is a senior non-commissioned army rank, so he is a soldier.

clue.text: Where finesse might come into play with this winding road

definitions.text: Where finesse might come into play

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with

indicators.note: winding means twisting about, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a drive is a road

explanation.surface: A twisting road demands deft handling.
explanation.walkthrough: Winding road reads as a phrase, but winding acts on the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A finesse is a card-play tactic, and a whist drive is a social evening of whist games.

clue.text: Coward wrote this irritating complaint

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a 1925 comedy by the playwright Noel Coward
second meaning: a pollen allergy that inflames eyes and nose

explanation.surface: A timid person penned something annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: Coward is not a timid person here but Noel Coward, the English playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Coward's play is also the common name for allergic rhinitis, an itchy seasonal ailment.

clue.text: Australian city delaying atomic contract

indicators.note: delaying pushes something later, so that letter is taken out and put back further along

parts.note: Darwin is the capital of Australia's Northern Territory
A is the abbreviation for atomic, as in A-bomb

explanation.surface: An Australian city puts off signing a nuclear deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The A of the city name is moved back two places: DARWIN becomes DRAWIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw in is to shrink or pull inward, as days draw in during autumn, so it means contract.

clue.text: Telegraph's newspaper covers with even number

indicators.note: covering something means wrapping around it

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times
this puzzle appears in the Telegraph, which would say our
e'en is the poetic contraction of even

explanation.surface: The Telegraph's paper reports with an even figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Even number looks like the definition, but even is wordplay and number alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Fourteen is a whole number, the one after thirteen.

clue.text: Leave telly on stand-by?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: depart on a journey
second meaning, read cryptically: a television set that is switched off

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: a TV set, not in use. Telly is British slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off is to start out or leave, and a set that is off describes an idle telly.

clue.text: "Parliament Upheld Law" — NY Times upcoming features

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means read from bottom to top
something featured is included within, so the letters sit inside the words

parts.note: letters spanning the words

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline reports that parliament upheld a law.
explanation.definitionFit: Tynwald is the parliament of the Isle of Man, one of the oldest continuous legislatures.

clue.text: Pitifully lazy, Yasmin cycles around collecting first of evening papers

indicators.note: going around and collecting means holding other letters inside
cycling moves the front letters round to the back while keeping their order

parts.note: the model Yasmin Le Bon, wife of Duran Duran's singer

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the next word is wanted

parts.note: opening letter
ID papers prove who you are

explanation.surface: A lazy Yasmin rides her bike about, picking up the evening paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Yasmin Le Bon is a British model; cycling moves her surname's first two letters to the back, and papers as ID is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Bone-idle means lazy to the bone, extremely and almost pitiably slothful.

clue.text: Plague George contracted first in Newgate cell

taken as written, then cut short

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the next word is wanted

parts.note: opening letter

explanation.surface: A man called George catches the plague in his cell in Newgate Prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Geo is the standard short form of George; Newgate was a notorious London prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is an underground prison cell, as found beneath castles.

clue.text: Worker who fills in?

parts.note: surface reading: a temp or stand-in who covers for absent staff
setter's reading: someone who puts fillings into teeth

explanation.walkthrough: Filling in suggests deputising; the trade is actually plugging cavities in teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist in mouth operations who also does fillings is a professional working on teeth.

clue.text: Restrained one crying half-heartedly

indicators.note: losing half the heart means dropping one of the two middle letters

parts.note: someone who sobs

explanation.surface: Someone tries to hold back tears but only half commits to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sober means sedate and restrained in manner, as in a sober suit.

clue.text: Clutch bag

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a travelling bag, an older word for a holdall

explanation.walkthrough: Clutch bag is a real type of handbag, but the words split into two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Grip means to hold firmly, and a grip is also a dated term for a small suitcase or holdall.

clue.text: Grumpy, cold and left stuck in Siberia shivering

indicators.note: things stuck in something are placed inside it
shivering shakes something about, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: Someone stranded, frozen and abandoned in Siberia is understandably bad-tempered.
explanation.definitionFit: Irascible describes a person easily angered, a near synonym of grumpy.

clue.text: Famous champion horse setting out runs good clip

indicators.note: setting things out means putting them aside, so those letters are removed

parts.note: Shergar won the 1981 Derby and was later kidnapped
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A famous racehorse heads out at a good speed.
explanation.walkthrough: Clip is a pace here in the surface, but it is the definition as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To shear is to cut or trim, as fleece is clipped from sheep.

clue.text: One of Haaland's strengths: commonly narrated Nordic works

explanation.walkthrough: Haaland, the Manchester City striker, scores with his head; a header said in Cockney style is 'eader.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edda is a pair of medieval Icelandic collections of Norse myth and poetry.

clue.text: Biscuit label, bluish-purple, the wrong way round

parts.note: pansy is a bluish-purple colour

explanation.definitionFit: A brandy snap is a thin rolled ginger biscuit, often filled with cream.
